source.title: The Impact of Parameter Scaling: Analysis of Specific Large Language Model Capabilities
source.authors: Ariya Uttama Putera; F. Marcellino; Sonya R. Manalu; Keenan Ario Muhamad

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates downstream task performance for language models of different parameter counts. It does not measure pretraining loss or fit scaling laws, so this is a different-measure test of V6.
record.gate_note: Rows record the local models' reported correct-answer totals and the paper's explicit category-level results. The paper's scaling-law equations and findings attributed to other studies are cited material, not results from this study. Inference speed is not included because it does not measure the claimed capability.
record.test_reason: The study scores nine locally run models (1B–20B) on six downstream questions, including within-family size sweeps (Llama3.2 1B/3B, Gemma3 1B/4B/12B, Qwen3 4B/8B). That bears on V6 with a different method from the originals. It measures no loss and fits no laws, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested. The evidence is very coarse: six binary items, a single run, and quantised models.
record.authors_conclusion:
The record's paraphrase is broadly correct but should be sharpened.
- The authors say model size remains decisive for complex reasoning and factual precision, with models under 4B often hallucinating or making math errors.
- They find diminishing gains from extra parameters for creative writing and basic language tasks.
- Training and data quality can outweigh scale: Qwen3 4B/8B beat Gemma3 12B and Mistral 7B, and Gemma3 12B was no better than 4B.
- They recommend 7B–8B models for 16GB-VRAM hardware.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates deployed models on a small set of downstream questions and aggregate correct-answer counts; it does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit power laws, or train runs at controlled parameter, token, and compute budgets.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors note that the small prompt set and single-shot tests are sensitive to phrasing; the evaluation used LM Studio defaults (temperature 0.8, top-p 0.8) without specific context system prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: Inference speed (tokens/s) falls with model size, and the authors frame this as an accuracy–speed trade-off on consumer hardware.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On fixed consumer hardware, larger local models trade inference speed for accuracy.

record.peer_reviewed: International Journal of Computer Science and Humanitarian AI, Vol. 3 No. 1 (February 2026)
record.problems: The authors acknowledge a narrow prompt set, binary pass/fail grading without partial credit, and single-shot tests sensitive to phrasing. The comparison spans different model families and does not control for training data, training method, architecture, or quantization. No uncertainty estimates are reported. Some category results are qualitative, and the text has a Llama 3.1/3.2 naming inconsistency.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for cloud models: the paper reports their results only in aggregate without per-model scores or stated parameter counts. Table 3 is a flattened table with ambiguous model-to-question assignments, so its checkmarks were not assigned to individual models. The cited scaling-law results are from other studies, not this study's own experiments.

untested.parts: All parts: pretraining loss is not measured.
All parts: no fits and no extrapolation.
All parts: compute allocation is not studied.
All parts: no shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
All parts: no other modalities or training regimes.
All parts: no exponents or fitting choices are examined.

missing.what: The authors claim a 'reasoning gap' between models of 3B and below and those of 8B and above. They also say models under 4B often hallucinate and make math errors. These are their own interpretive scale claims, and no row records them.

record.verdict_notes:
Label changes from the record:
- The record's 'challenges' label is downgraded to limits_scope. The flat segments come from six pass/fail items over small size ratios, so they cannot establish absence.
- Qwen3 4B/8B sit at ceiling and the comparison cannot be read.
- The record's methodological limits_scope label is dropped, because it describes study quality, not results.

Problems with the evidence:
- Cross-family comparisons are confounded by training data, recipe and quantisation, so the single-size rows (r6, r9, r13) and r15 stay cannot_determine.
- The paper is internally inconsistent. It says 'eight local models' but lists nine, and refers to 'two questions every class' though only one per class is shown. Its recommendation of Mistral 7B conflicts with Mistral's lowest score (3/6).
- The study is peer-reviewed in a small journal.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law form and range.
Whether fits from small training runs predict loss on much larger runs.
Compute-budget allocation, optimal parameter and token counts, and their trends with compute.
Controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests task scores across parameter counts, but not downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss, broad task benchmarks, or predictability across many scales and runs.
It does not fit or compare scaling-law exponents, investigate fitting choices, or measure loss-curve bending.

rows.subject: Local models (aggregate; nine model sizes)
rows.operation_detail: Tested on the mathematics and logical reasoning question.
rows.value: Five of nine model sizes answered correctly; the text says four gave abstract and imprecise reasoning.
rows.note: The report gives an aggregate count, not a size-stratified trend; its listed failing models include a Llama 3.1 name although the evaluated family is listed as Llama 3.2.
rows.check: The data are size-stratified after all. Section 4.1.1 names the failing models as Llama 1B and 3B, Gemma3 1B and Mistral 7B. Gemma3 4B and 12B, Qwen3 4B and 8B, and GPT-oss 20B passed. So within Gemma, 1B fails and the larger sizes pass, while within Llama both sizes fail. The text writes 'Llama 3.1 (1B)', most likely a typo for 3.2.

rows.subject: Llama3.2
rows.value: The paper says both sizes were lacking: they focused on analysis and did not answer the question or its possibilities.
rows.note: The outcome is reported for both sizes together and does not provide a parameter-scaled score.
rows.check: Both Llama3.2 sizes fail the ambiguity question, so this within-family pair shows no gain from 1B to 3B.

relationships.reason: The total score rises from 4/6 to 5/6, and the 4B model passes the math item that 1B fails (r3, r4, r10).
relationships.display_finding: The total score increased from 4/6 to 5/6, with the larger model passing the previously failed math item.

relationships.condition: Llama3.2 1B → 3B and Gemma3 4B → 12B; the hallucination, ambiguity and creativity items
relationships.reason: Scores are flat within these size steps: Llama 4/6 at both sizes, Gemma 5/6 at both. All Gemma sizes hallucinate, both Llama sizes fail ambiguity, and creativity is similar across all models. This rests on six binary items (r1, r2, r4, r5, r11, r12, r14).
relationships.display_finding: Llama stayed at 4/6 and Gemma at 5/6 across the size steps; all Gemma sizes hallucinated, both Llama sizes failed ambiguity, and creativity remained similar on the six binary items.
